sections.title: Executive investment summary: a state warship yard at peak execution and trough order intake

subsections.title: What the company actually does, in plain terms

blocks.text: Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Ltd (GRSE) is a central public sector shipyard under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence that designs and builds warships for the Indian Navy and Indian Coast Guard, and increasingly non-defence vessels for other arms of the Indian state and a small number of foreign commercial owners [F] (AR2025 p.81). It is a **platform integrator**: the hull is fabricated in-house, while roughly 65% of a ship's cost is equipment and systems, most of which is nominated by the customer and bought in [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Revenue is recognised over time on an input (cost-to-cost) basis as construction progresses, not on delivery [F] (AR2025 p.141).

The company runs three disclosed divisions. In FY25 the Ship Division produced Rs 4,870.85 cr of value of production, the Engineering Division (Bailey-type portable steel bridges, deck machinery) Rs 149.79 cr and the Engine Division (marine diesel engines assembled at Ranchi under an MTU, Germany collaboration) Rs 50.34 cr [F] (AR2025 p.38). For FY26 the rating agency reports the mix as shipbuilding 93%, ship repair 4% and engineering 3% of revenue [F] (RATING). A fourth vertical - a 30 mm Naval Surface Gun built under a Rs 248.50 cr MoD contract with 60% indigenous content - was added in FY24 [F] (AR2025 p.43).

End-market split is disclosed only through the order book, not through audited segment revenue. As at 30 Jun 2026 the order book was Rs 13,596 cr, of which shipbuilding was Rs 12,980 cr (about 95%); within shipbuilding, four Indian Navy projects accounted for about 74% and non-defence about 25% [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The credit rating report puts roughly 76% of the Mar 2026 order book with the Indian Navy and Coast Guard, about 21% commercial shipbuilding and export, and the remainder ship repair and engineering [F] (RATING).

Geography is overwhelmingly domestic. Export revenue (value of production) was Rs 73.63 cr in FY25, about 1.5% of a Rs 5,071 cr total [F] (AR2025 p.43). Management stated exports exceeded Rs 270 cr in FY26 [MC] (CALL May 2026), which on Rs 7,002 cr of revenue would be about 3.9% [E] (NUMBERS). All shipbuilding is done from four yards in and around Kolkata plus an engine plant at Ranchi [F] (AR2025 p.104).

Listing status: GRSE is not a recent listing. Its shares were listed on NSE and BSE on 10 Oct 2018 [F] (RATING). The evidence base is therefore a full listed-company record - eight years of exchange filings, annual reports, four earnings-call transcripts and a credit rating - not a prospectus. What is genuinely missing is audited segment reporting: as a defence producer GRSE is exempted from Ind AS 108 by MCA notification S.O. 802(E) dated 23 Feb 2018, and the auditor records this exemption explicitly in its opinion [F] (AR2025 p.143, p.178). No investor presentation more recent than Jun 2019 was available in this folder, and no FY26 annual report - the latest full annual report is FY25.

blocks.text: Classifying the drivers: #2 (qualified-yard status) and #5 (net-cash, state-backed balance sheet) are **structural**. #1, #4, #6, #7 and #8 are **company-specific** - they depend on GRSE's own execution and its own capex, and can be competed away or mis-executed. #3 is **cyclical/policy-driven**: it is a function of the naval acquisition cycle and the current fiscal posture, and the same DAC process that creates the pipeline has already slipped one Rs 33,000 cr contract by more than a year [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Aug 2026) [AI].

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the ten strongest reasons not to own it

items: **1. The order book has halved in fifteen months and net new intake has been close to zero.** Order book: Rs 22,681 cr at 31 Mar 2025 [F] (AR2025 p.44); Rs 20,206 cr at 30 Sep 2025; Rs 18,482 cr at 31 Dec 2025; Rs 15,324 cr at 31 Mar 2026; Rs 13,596 cr at 30 Jun 2026 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025, CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). FY26 revenue was Rs 7,002 cr while the order book fell Rs 7,357 cr, implying essentially nil - arithmetically slightly negative - net order inflow for the whole of FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). In Q1 FY27 the book fell Rs 1,728 cr against Rs 1,815 cr of revenue, implying roughly Rs 87 cr of net inflow in the quarter [E] (NUMBERS, CALL Aug 2026). Management frames the decline as a compliment to execution [MC] (CALL Aug 2026); arithmetically it is also a statement about intake [AI].

**2. Management guided to a Rs 50,000 cr order book at FY26 year-end and delivered Rs 15,324 cr.** The guidance was given twice - 'confident of ending the financial year with an order book plus Rs 50,000 crores' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) and repeated in Feb 2026 [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). This was contingent on the Next Generation Corvette contract, which has now slipped from 'next 3 to 4 months' (Nov 2025), to 'next month' (Feb 2026), to 'the current quarter that is June' (May 2026), to 'this quarter' (Aug 2026) [MC] (CALL Nov 2025, CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). Four consecutive dates, all missed.

**3. Even once signed, the NGC contributes nothing to revenue until FY28 and materially only from FY29.** 'The first revenue recognition will commence next year, that is the Financial Year 2028' and 'the major chunk of the revenue recognition will start from FY29' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL May 2026). Meanwhile the two projects carrying the current P&L - P-17A (Rs 4,519 cr remaining) and ASW-SWC (Rs 1,815 cr remaining) - are both scheduled to complete in FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The FY28-29 revenue bridge rests on base-and-depot spares, one-off research vessels and orders not yet won.

**4. Cash does not follow profit.** Cumulative operating cash flow was -0.60x reported profit over the last three years [E] (NUMBERS). CFO was -Rs 707 cr (FY24), +Rs 16 cr (FY25) and -Rs 290 cr (FY26) against PAT of Rs 357 cr, Rs 527 cr and Rs 748 cr. Free cash flow was negative in four of the last five years, cumulatively -Rs 176 cr over five years and -Rs 1,173 cr over three [F] (NUMBERS).

**5. Reported margin improvement has an explicit non-operating component.** The FY25 auditor's report carries an Emphasis of Matter on Note 48: revising cost-to-completion estimates on P-17A and NGOPV reduced estimated cost to completion by Rs 433.03 cr and increased FY25 profit by Rs 100 cr [F] (AR2025 p.141, p.199) - about 19% of FY25 PAT [E]. The rating agency states the FY26 margin also benefited from 'reversal of excess cost provisions created in earlier years' [F] (RATING). An analyst asked directly whether sustainable margin is nearer 9.5-10%; management would only repeat 'we will be able to maintain similar margins' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**6. A quarter of pre-tax profit is interest on someone else's money, and that money is running down.** Other income was 27.3% of FY26 PBT and 28.1% of TTM PBT [E] (NUMBERS). Interest income was Rs 246 cr in FY26 [F] (RATING), earned largely on customer stage payments: contract liabilities were Rs 6,900 cr at 31 Mar 2025, down from Rs 7,327 cr [F] (AR2025 p.177), and cash fell from Rs 3,732 cr to Rs 3,511 cr over FY26 [F] (RATING). As the order book runs off, both the float and the interest on it shrink.

**7. There is no pricing power and no pass-through.** Every current contract is fixed price and every order to subcontractors is fixed price [MC] (CALL May 2026). The rating agency lists 'fixed-price contracts with fluctuating margins' as the single key weakness [F] (RATING). Management says commodity inflation has 'minimal impact' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026), and the FY25 corporate governance report states the company 'had no exposure to commodity and commodity risks' for the year and does no hedging [F] (AR2025 p.103) - a claim that is not reconciled with the rating agency's weakness assessment [AI].

**8. Q1 FY27 margin came in well below the guided level.** Q1 FY27 EBITDA was Rs 149 cr on Rs 1,815 cr of sales, an 8.2% margin, against 16.8% in Q4 FY26 and 11.4% for FY26 [E] (NUMBERS). PAT of Rs 173 cr included Rs 100 cr of other income - 43% of the Rs 232 cr PBT [E] (NUMBERS). Management explained the quarter-on-quarter cost fall by commissioning activity in the prior quarter, not by a margin view [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**9. Governance is structurally constrained and the company has been fined for it.** GRSE did not have the requisite number of Independent Directors or any Woman Independent Director through FY25; the Audit Committee was unconstituted from 27 Dec 2024 to 31 Mar 2025 and the HR/Nomination and Remuneration Committee from 11 Dec 2024 to 31 Mar 2025 [F] (AR2025 p.61). Cumulative exchange fines disclosed are Rs 1.20 cr (NSE) and Rs 1.10 cr (BSE) since FY21, unpaid and under waiver request [F] (AR2025 p.99-100). The company's explanation - that board appointments are made by the Government of India - is correct and is precisely the point: minority shareholders have no lever [AI].

**10. The capex plan is not reconciled between the company and its rating agency.** Management describes about Rs 200 cr on two brownfield yards, about Rs 2,200 cr on the Raichak greenfield and about Rs 2,000 cr on a Gujarat total-ship-solution facility - roughly Rs 4,400 cr in total [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The rating agency, writing on 22 Jun 2026, records 'the company's planned Rs 500-600 crore capex in the next two years towards expansion of its shipbuilding capacity through two brownfield and two greenfield facilities' [F] (RATING). These two statements are not reconciled. Historic capex has run at Rs 42-77 cr a year, 1.1-1.6% of sales [F] (NUMBERS).

subsections.title: Key debates: what the market may be getting wrong, in both directions

blocks.caption: Live debates and how the evidence cuts

It reflects an execution rate that has roughly doubled; the book fell because ships were delivered, and the pipeline behind it is Rs 1,50,000 cr [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)
Book-to-bill has been at or below 1.0x for five consecutive quarters; a pipeline is not a backlog [E] (NUMBERS)

Both are true simultaneously. Execution did improve. But net intake in FY26 was approximately nil, and coverage fell from 4.5 years of FY25 revenue to 1.8 years of TTM revenue [E] (NUMBERS, AR2025 p.44). The debate resolves entirely on NGC signature and P-17 Bravo [AI]
Scale and fixed-cost absorption on a Rs 7,000 cr revenue base are genuinely structural; ROCE at 43% supports this [F] (RATING, NUMBERS)
Rs 100 cr of the FY25 uplift came from a cost-to-complete revision; FY26 benefited from provision reversals; Q1 FY27 printed 8.2% [F] (AR2025 p.199, RATING), [E] (NUMBERS)

The scale effect is real; the increment above roughly 9-10% is not yet demonstrated as recurring. Management declined three separate invitations to confirm a sustainable level [MC] (CALL May 2026) [AI]

Non-defence is already about a quarter of the shipbuilding book and European owners are actively approaching Indian yards [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026)

Management says explicitly that the first commercial contracts were taken at thin or subsidised margins for entry, and that 'the money and the margins are very much within warship building' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025, CALL May 2026)
Diversification of counterparty risk is real; diversification of profit is not yet. GRSE has also consciously stopped taking export orders to prioritise domestic demand [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)
Does capacity constrain growth, or does order intake?
Capacity is being raised from 28 to 32 to 43 concurrent platforms, and management says current capacity 'would be inadequate to meet the huge demand' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)

The yard was carrying 40 vessels under construction in FY25 against a stated 28-platform capacity, largely via outsourcing to partner yards [F] (AR2025 p.40), [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The binding constraint in FY26-27 is orders, not berths [AI]
On today's evidence the constraint is intake. Capacity becomes the constraint only if the Rs 1,50,000 cr pipeline converts - which is the bull case, not the base case [AI]
Does Navratna status change the economics?
It grants autonomy for investment decisions without case-by-case ministry approval, enabling the expansion plan [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)

No quantified financial benefit has been disclosed. The same board is still appointed by Presidential Order, and the same corporate actions (bonus, split) still await DIPAM direction [MC] (CALL Aug 2026)
Procedural upgrade with real optionality on capex speed; no evidence of a P&L effect [AI]

blocks.text: The consensus frame treats GRSE as a defence-capex compounder whose Rs 1,50,000 cr addressable pipeline makes the current order book a technicality. Our read is that GRSE is better understood as a **single-buyer, fixed-price project business in the late innings of one contract cycle and waiting on the first contract of the next**. The FY26 print - 38% revenue growth, 11.45% margin, 43% ROCE - is the peak output of a book that was signed in 2019-2023, and management itself flagged FY27 as 'the peak year' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The three things that determine whether the next cycle is as good are outside the company's control: DAC timelines, the NGC signature and the P-17 Bravo RFP. Meanwhile the financial signature of a business converting backlog into revenue without replacing it is already visible - working capital days have compressed from -1,012 in FY21 to -80 in FY26 as customer advances drain, cash has fallen from Rs 3,732 cr to Rs 3,511 cr, and CFO was -Rs 290 cr in a year of Rs 748 cr reported profit [F] (NUMBERS, RATING). Against that, the price implies roughly 65% annual sales growth for five years [E] (NUMBERS). The variant view is not that the business is bad - it is that the market is paying a growth-compounder multiple for an execution-cycle business at the top of its execution cycle [AI].

blocks.text: The auditor confirms under CARO that the company has no subsidiary, joint venture or associate [F] (AR2025 p.146), and the corporate governance report confirms the same while noting a Policy on Determining Material Subsidiaries exists as a formality [F] (AR2025 p.98). GRSE has, however, signed a number of non-equity collaboration MoUs: Larsen & Toubro Ltd (commercial vessels), Swan Defence (large platforms above 250 m), Hindustan Shipyard Ltd (a consortium agreement for the LPD project), SHM Shipcare, Merlinhawk Aerospace, KELTRON, Naval Group S.A. of France, Apollo Micro Systems, Medha Servo Systems, Conceptia Software and IOE Offshore [F] (AR2025 p.44), [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). An MoU with the Andhra Pradesh Maritime Board for a greenfield facility was signed and then abandoned; management described it candidly as 'we were fishing... then we backtracked because we found it was not required' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). None of these MoUs has a disclosed order value or economic contribution.

GRSE is 92 years old as a corporate entity and 66 years old as a state warship yard, but **the business that generates today's numbers is about seven years old**. Sales were Rs 921 cr in FY17 and Rs 1,141 cr in FY21; they are Rs 7,507 cr on a trailing basis [F] (NUMBERS). The entire scale-up traces to two contract signatures in FY19-20 - the P-17A frigate programme (awarded on nomination) and the eight-ship ASW-SWC programme signed 29 Apr 2019 at Rs 6,311.32 cr [F] (PPT Jun 2019) - plus the Survey Vessel Large programme. Both of those programmes complete in FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

The corollary matters for underwriting. Nine-year sales CAGR is 25.3%, five-year 43.7% and three-year 39.8% [F] (NUMBERS) - but these are not a compounding growth series, they are the ramp of a small number of large, discrete contracts through the steep part of a shipbuilding S-curve. The 2019 investor presentation shows a company doing Rs 1,386 cr of turnover with a Rs 21,644 cr order book [F] (PPT Jun 2019). Today it does Rs 7,507 cr with a Rs 13,596 cr order book. The revenue has grown 5.4x while the backlog has fallen 37% [E]. That is what the end of a cycle looks like, and it is the single most important fact the timeline discloses [AI].

sections.title: The production chain and where value is captured

subsections.title: The shipbuilding chain, step by step

items: **1. Approval of Necessity (AoN).** The Defence Acquisition Council accords AoN for a class of platform, setting an indicative value. GRSE does not participate; it is a customer-side gate [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

**2. RFP and competitive bid.** Management states that every order today is competitive except work won from foreign clients: 'there was a time when, before we were listed, we used to take the system for granted that orders used to come aplenty on nomination. Now every order... is on competition' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The exception in the current book is P-17A, awarded on nomination [F] (RATING).

**3. L1 declaration, price negotiation, contract.** Elapsed time from bid to contract is disclosed as roughly six months for small projects and nine to twelve months for large ones [MC] (CALL May 2026). The NGC has taken longer: tender out August, L1 October, still unsigned more than a year later [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Aug 2026).

**4. Pre-production / design phase.** Design studies, equipment specification freeze and downstream ordering. Revenue recognition in this phase is 5-10% of project cost; management expects first downstream OEM orders within three to six months of contract signature [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL May 2026).

**5. Hull fabrication and block construction.** Steel cutting, block fabrication, keel laying, launch. Wholly indigenous - 'float' is about 10% of ship cost and 100% indigenised [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Non-core block fabrication and welding are outsourced to a Kolkata subcontracted vendor base [MC] (CALL Feb 2026); sub-contracting charges were Rs 483.57 cr in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.152).

**6. Equipment procurement and integration.** About 65% of a ship's cost is equipment and systems, largely customer-nominated; within that, on the NGC, 55-60% is weapons, sensors and electronics (mainly Bharat Electronics) and 40-45% machinery and propulsion [MC] (CALL May 2026). This is the steep part of the revenue-recognition curve.

**7. Outfitting, basin trials, contractor sea trials, delivery.** Payment follows a 15-stage schedule under the Defence Acquisition Procedure, with the 14th stage at delivery and the 15th after a one-year warranty [MC] (CALL May 2026). No advance is taken - management says 'I don't want any advance... I want a stage payment' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**8. Base-and-depot spares and warranty.** Ten-plus percent of project cost sits in base-and-depot spares contracted separately and delivered after ship handover, extending revenue beyond the delivery date [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). A guarantee-repair provision of Rs 19.11 cr was carried at 31 Mar 2025 [F] (AR2025 p.177).

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and why

blocks.text: Value is captured at the integration stage, not at the component stage. Because roughly 65% of ship cost is customer-nominated equipment, GRSE is largely a pass-through on the most expensive part of its own product [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The measure that matters is therefore value added, and GRSE discloses it: value added was Rs 1,479.75 cr on value of production of Rs 5,070.98 cr in FY25 - 29% - down from 37% in FY23 and FY24, 46% in FY22 and 59% in FY21 [F] (AR2025 p.27, p.38). **Value added as a share of production has fallen every year for four years while revenue grew.** That is exactly what you would expect as equipment-heavy phases of the P-17A and ASW-SWC programmes dominate; it is not evidence of margin destruction, but it does mean the growth is disproportionately bought-in content [AI].

Capital intensity is low by the standards of heavy manufacturing but the working-capital intensity is extreme and negative. Gross block was Rs 816.18 cr at 31 Mar 2025 against Rs 5,071 cr of production [F] (AR2025 p.38); fixed-asset turnover has risen from 2.57x (FY17) to 12.16x (FY26) [F] (NUMBERS). Capex has run at 1.1-1.6% of sales for three years [F] (NUMBERS). The asset that actually funds the business is customer stage payments: contract liabilities of Rs 6,900 cr at 31 Mar 2025, against total assets of Rs 10,354 cr [F] (AR2025 p.151, p.177). GRSE is, financially, an asset-light integrator funded by its customer - which works beautifully while the order book is growing and works against you when it is not [AI].

Outsourcing is used deliberately as a capacity release valve. subsections.title: Why each segment moved, and our read

items: **Ship Division +44% in FY25 and +38% in FY26.** Management: 'we are in an execution phase... last year we have delivered eight ships, so naturally when the ships are delivered, the revenue and in turn the profits would increase' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The rating agency attributes FY26 growth 'mainly led by execution of frigates P-17A' [F] (RATING). **Our read [AI]:** correct as far as it goes, but this is S-curve mathematics, not demand growth. The same two projects that produced the FY25-27 revenue peak also produce the FY28 hole, because both close in FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Engineering Division -10% in FY25.** No explanation is given in the annual report; production actually rose from 90 bridges (6,750 MT) to 102 bridges (7,715 MT) while VoP fell from Rs 167.17 cr to Rs 149.79 cr [F] (AR2025 p.21, p.42). **Our read [AI]:** volume up, value down implies either mix shift to lighter spans or realisation decline. Not disclosed. The division then recovered strongly, exceeding Rs 200 cr in FY26 including 30 export bridges [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Engine Division +5% in FY25.** Completed delivery of all 28 diesel alternators for the P-17A project to MDL and GRSE, and one MTU 4000 series engine to the Coast Guard; a Rs 4.37 cr test-bed upgrade was completed [F] (AR2025 p.43). **Our read [AI]:** sub-scale and project-dependent; Rs 82 cr of order book at Jun 2026 is under two months of group revenue [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Ship Repair from Rs 19 cr (FY22) to Rs 113.82 cr (FY25) to ~4% of FY26 revenue.** Driven by the Oct 2021 concession for three Khidderpore dry docks from Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port [F] (AR2025 p.81). Management says margins here are high and that GRSE has deliberately not scaled it yet [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **Our read [AI]:** this is the most interesting under-exploited line in the company, and also the one with the least disclosure - no repair margin, no utilisation, no contract list.

**Naval Surface Gun: first revenue of Rs 32 cr in FY25.** Against a Rs 248.50 cr contract signed May 2023 [F] (AR2025 p.43). A liquidated-damages contingent liability of Rs 4.80 cr was recognised on this contract because the delivery-date extension is still awaiting Navy approval [F] (AR2025 p.183). **Our read [AI]:** the first weapons programme is late, which is normal, but the LD disclosure is a reminder that every fixed-price contract carries a penalty tail.

blocks.text: **Order-driven versus organic.** Shipbuilding, research vessels, the gun and deck machinery are entirely order-driven: nothing is produced without a signed contract and a stage-payment schedule. Bailey bridges are the closest thing GRSE has to an organic, repeat-order business - MoUs with the Indian Army, BRO and NHIDCL generate recurring demand, and 13 bridge sets were delivered to Uttarakhand PWD in one month for flood restoration [F] (AR2025 p.42). Ship repair is semi-organic - fleet maintenance is a recurring requirement, but each refit is separately tendered [F] (AR2025 p.42). No segment margins are disclosed for any of these.

items: **Currency exposure.** The company states it is exposed to foreign exchange on procurement of materials and services, but that 'these procurements are mostly covered under exchange rate variation clause for reimbursement of exchange rate variations arising out of foreign currency fluctuations. Hence, your Company has no direct exposure on this account' [F] (AR2025 p.103). It does not hedge [F] (AR2025 p.103). Net foreign exchange gains of Rs 7.72 cr were recorded in other income in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.179). **Our read [AI]:** the ERV clause covers defence contracts with the Indian state; the USD-denominated export contracts with a German owner and Bangladesh agencies carry receipt-side currency exposure whose treatment is not separately disclosed.

**Trade and tariff policy.** No tariff exposure is disclosed anywhere in the documents. The relevant policy exposure runs the other way: the rating agency cites 'extension of customs duty exemptions on shipbuilding inputs' as an industry support measure [F] (RATING). A live customs dispute exists - the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, Kakinada, has raised a demand of Rs 4.02 cr including interest, asserting that imported drawings for the Bangladesh dredger did not qualify for nil duty; GRSE has not acknowledged the demand [F] (AR2025 p.183).

**Government policy dates.** The shipbuilding revitalisation package of Rs 69,725 cr comprises Rs 24,736 cr of Shipbuilding Financial Assistance (15-30% subsidy by platform type), Rs 4,001 cr of Shipbuilding and Shipbreaking Credit Note, Rs 25,000 cr Maritime Development Fund, about Rs 5,000 cr of interest subvention and Rs 19,989 cr for maritime clusters including up to 50% subsidy for greenfield facilities [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). A draft Defence Acquisition Procedure 2026 was open for public comment as of Feb 2026, with an expected focus on indigenisation incentives and public-private entry [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). None of these has produced a quantified benefit to GRSE in any disclosed period.

blocks.text: **Single-location manufacturing risk is acute and the company says so itself.** All shipbuilding is in Kolkata: Main Works Unit and Rajabagan Dockyard (build), Fitting Out Jetty, 61 Park and Taratala (engineering), with the engine plant at Ranchi [F] (AR2025 p.104). The company's own SWOT lists as weaknesses: 'Constraints of a riverine shipyard due to limitations in the depth and width of navigable channels with effects of silting in rivers'; 'Location of the company in densely populated residential areas having narrow roads'; and 'Weak shipbuilding ecosystem in the eastern part of India' [F] (AR2025 p.81). Current capability is capped at about 10,000 t displacement and 200 m length, which excludes most large commercial vessels [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The entire greenfield programme - Raichak and Gujarat - exists to fix this, and is three to five years from operation [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Customer concentration by revenue is not disclosed in any period.** GRSE publishes no top-1, top-5 or top-10 customer revenue table. Because it is a government company under the control of the Ministry of Defence, it has availed the Ind AS 24 exemption from detailed related-party disclosure for transactions with government and government-related entities [F] (AR2025 p.189). The individually significant related-party transactions that are disclosed (sale of goods Rs 873.81 cr, sale of services Rs 57.61 cr in FY25) cover entities owned by the Government of India - i.e. other PSUs - and therefore do not capture the Indian Navy relationship at all [F] (AR2025 p.190). blocks.text: **Disclosed case studies.** Two are given in detail. First, the German multi-purpose vessel relationship: 'we took nearly six months to get into the first contract for the four vessels of the German client. Then the next four and the next four came almost back-to-back... it is just a question of making the break' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **Long-term agreements versus purchase orders.** Defence work runs on multi-year fixed-price contracts with 15-stage payment schedules under the Defence Acquisition Procedure, not on purchase orders [MC] (CALL May 2026). GRSE holds a three-year contract with the Indian Navy for capstan product support, and a 15-year MoU with the naval gun collaboration partners [F] (AR2025 p.43). Bridge work runs on MoUs with the Army, BRO and NHIDCL that frame but do not guarantee volume [F] (AR2025 p.44). Commercial export work is contract-by-contract.

**Is concentration improving or worsening? Both, depending on the measure.** By counterparty count, it is improving: the shipbuilding order book has gone from about 98-99% defence to about 75% in roughly three years, and the customer list now includes three different ministries, a state government, a foreign shipowner and a foreign port authority [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [F] (PPT Jun 2019). By economic exposure, it is not: the four naval projects still carry 71% of the book and the single largest, P-17A, was 38% of the March 2026 book [F] (RATING); revenue concentration is undisclosed in every period; and essentially all the non-defence diversification is to other arms of the same sovereign - Ministry of Earth Sciences, DRDO, Geological Survey of India, a state government. subsections.title: Overall read on the client base

blocks.text: Four observations. **First**, the stickiest relationships (Navy, Coast Guard, BRO) are also the ones with the least pricing power - management's own framing is that price negotiation happens once, against a single buyer, and margin is then an execution problem [MC] (CALL May 2026, on fixed-price contracts). **Second**, wallet share with the Navy is not really a lever, because the Navy buys programmes, not incremental volume - GRSE either wins the P-17 Bravo or it does not, and management frames it as binary: 'that is what will keep the company moving for another 10 years, 8 years' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). **Third**, the newest and fastest-growing relationships (the German owner, ONGC, the port) are individually small and, in the German case, deliberately paused. **Fourth**, and most important for forecasting: of the nine client groups above, only two - bridges and ship repair - generate recurring, non-programme revenue, and together they are under 8% of the business [E] (RATING, AR2025 p.42). This is a project business with a state anchor tenant, not an installed-base business [AI].

GRSE discloses an order book figure at every quarterly interaction and an audited-year figure in the annual report, plus a project-level breakdown on request. It does not disclose order intake, cancellations, price escalations or the split between firm contracts and letters of intent. The order book at 30 Jun 2026 was Rs 13,596.26 cr across 11 projects and 44 marine platforms [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Management's own framing of the decline: 'it is for the first time in the last 10 years that our order book has dropped below Rs 15,000 crore and I consider it the reflection of an excellent execution rate' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

subsections.title: 1. Naval shipbuilding - where GRSE sits and what the FY28 gap really is

blocks.text: **Position in the value chain.** GRSE is a tier-1 prime integrator: it holds the contract with the Ministry of Defence, owns the design (for classes it has built) and integrates equipment procured from a downstream ecosystem. Downstream of GRSE sit Bharat Electronics (the dominant electronics supplier - on NGC, about 65% of project cost is equipment and of that 55-60% is weapons, sensors and electronics), HAL (marine gas turbines, routed from abroad), ECIL, Keltron, plus L&T, Adani, Mahindra and Kalyani in the private sector, and a stated national ecosystem of about 17,000 MSMEs, 1,000 startups and 675 innovators [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). Upstream sits a single sovereign buyer whose procurement rules (Defence Acquisition Procedure) set the payment schedule, the specification and the competitive field.

**What exists today versus narrative.** What exists: four Kolkata yards with capacity for 28 concurrent platforms up to 10,000 t and 200 m; a delivered record of 118 warships; two large programmes 74-91% complete; indigenisation of about 80-85% by value across recent projects, with float 100%, fight about 60%, survive about 70% and move (propulsion engines) still import-dependent [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [F] (RATING). What is narrative: the capacity to build large commercial vessels (requires partners or the unbuilt greenfield yards); autonomous platforms (prototypes proved, one USV delivered to DRDO, no production contract); and the Rs 1,50,000 cr pipeline (no contract).

**Government/anchor-customer exposure, quantified.** The Government of India holds 74.50% of the equity through the President of India [F] (AR2025 p.103). The Ministry of Defence appoints the entire board [F] (RATING). About 71-76% of the order book is Navy and Coast Guard [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [F] (RATING). The remaining 'non-defence' work is overwhelmingly to other government entities - Ministry of Earth Sciences, DRDO, Geological Survey of India, a state government, a port authority, a state oil company. Genuinely non-government exposure is one German shipowner and one Bangladeshi authority, together roughly 10% of the order book [E] (CALL Aug 2026).

blocks.text: **Utilisation is not disclosed in any period, in any document.** GRSE publishes no capacity-utilisation percentage, no tonnage capacity, no CGT figure and no berth-days statistic. The only quantity that can be compared to the stated capacity is the number of platforms under construction - and it exceeds the stated capacity. The FY25 annual report shows 40 vessels under construction against a stated concurrent capacity of 28 [F] (AR2025 p.16, p.40); the Feb 2026 call describes 42 platforms in 10 projects [MC] (CALL Feb 2026); the Aug 2026 call describes 44 marine platforms in 11 projects [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The reconciling item is outsourcing: under a public-private partnership model, seven platforms were offloaded in whole or at 75% construction to a large private yard (five taken out) and two more from a smaller yard [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Because neither the platform mix nor the outsourced share is quantified, **no meaningful utilisation rate can be computed from the disclosures**, and we decline to invent one.

**Why 'utilisation' changed, in the sense that can be observed.** The only observable proxy is fixed-asset turnover, which rose from 3.36x (FY21) to 5.04x (FY23) to 7.29x (FY24) to 9.86x (FY25) to 12.16x (FY26) [F] (NUMBERS). Value of production per employee rose from Rs 65.66 lakh in FY19 to about Rs 3.00 cr in FY25 [F] (PPT Jun 2019); [E] (AR2025 p.27, p.38), on a headcount that fell from 2,100 to 1,690. Management attributes throughput gains to integrated construction methodology, the Virtual Reality Laboratory, PDM/PLM systems, robotic welding and plasma cutting, and AI-enabled weld-defect identification [F] (AR2025 p.34, p.47). Our read [AI]: the productivity gain is real but is dominated by revenue mix - the equipment-lowering phase of two large frigate and corvette programmes carries a very high revenue-to-fixed-asset ratio and a low value-added ratio. Value added fell from 59% of production (FY21) to 29% (FY25) over exactly the period fixed-asset turnover tripled [F] (AR2025 p.27).

**Revenue potential from higher utilisation - sensitivity, not a base case [E].** Because utilisation is not disclosed, the only defensible sensitivity is the platform count. If the yard moves from 28 to 32 concurrent platforms as management guides by end-CY2026, that is a 14.3% increase in the stated capacity unit [E] (CALL Aug 2026). If revenue scaled linearly with concurrent platforms from the TTM base of Rs 7,507 cr, the implied uplift would be about Rs 1,073 cr of annual revenue [E] (NUMBERS). **This is a sensitivity and not a forecast.** Revenue in shipbuilding is a function of where each platform sits on its S-curve, not of how many berths are occupied; and on today's evidence the binding constraint is order intake, not berths. We would not carry this into a base case.

**Lease expiries.** The three Khidderpore dry docks are held under a concession agreement with Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port dated 7 Oct 2021; the term is not disclosed [F] (AR2025 p.81). The Raichak greenfield land is held on 'a very long-term lease from Kolkata Port Trust' with no term disclosed [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The accounts show a land lease liability of Rs 6.56 cr with undiscounted maturities of Rs 17.17 cr beyond five years, implying a long tail, and annual land rent of Rs 0.55 cr [F] (AR2025 p.197). No lease expiry date is disclosed anywhere in the documents.

But the reading has to be honest about mechanism [AI]. The growth did not come from installed capacity; it came from executing an order book that was already signed, and from a revenue mix in which roughly 65-70% of cost is bought-in equipment that never touches GRSE's fixed assets. subsections.title: Planned capex and how it is funded

blocks.text: **The two authoritative sources on planned capex differ by roughly seven times and are not reconciled.** The credit rating agency, writing 22 Jun 2026, records 'the company's planned Rs 500-600 crore capex in the next two years towards expansion of its shipbuilding capacity through two brownfield and two greenfield facilities in West Bengal and Gujarat, to be funded primarily through internal accruals and liquidity' [F] (RATING). Six weeks later, on 6 Aug 2026, the CMD described about Rs 200 cr for the two leased brownfield facilities over 18 months, about Rs 2,200 cr for the Raichak greenfield and about Rs 2,000 cr for the Gujarat facility - roughly Rs 4,400 cr [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Both may be internally consistent if the rating agency is describing only the two-year cash outlay while management describes the full multi-year project cost, but neither source says so, and the reconciliation is not disclosed.

items: **Funding.** Both sources point to internal accruals and existing liquidity, not debt [F] (RATING). GRSE had Rs 3,511 cr of cash and bank balances at 31 Mar 2026 and nil term debt [F] (RATING). The rating agency's negative trigger includes any reduction in liquid funds below Rs 3,000 cr on a continued basis [F] (RATING) - which is a live constraint if the full Rs 4,400 cr programme proceeds from internal resources [AI].

**Subsidy.** Management expects to leverage the Rs 69,725 cr government package, which includes up to 50% subsidy for greenfield cluster facilities and a Maritime Development Fund covering a share of brownfield investment [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). No subsidy has been received or quantified in any disclosed period; the auditor confirms that during FY25 no grant, subsidy or assistance was received from Central or State Government [F] (AR2025 p.148).

**Timing.** Brownfield: production from end of calendar 2026 for two sites, plus a larger third site needing two years [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Raichak: approvals in CY2026, build from 2027, three to five years to full operation [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Gujarat: DPR complete and environmental clearance obtained, project commences 2027, about three years to operation [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). None of this affects FY27 or FY28 revenue.

**Historical precedent on capex guidance.** The Jun 2019 investor presentation stated that the shipyard planned to spend Rs 200-250 cr over the following three to four years on modernisation [F] (PPT Jun 2019). Actual capex FY20-FY23 was Rs 329 cr [E] (NUMBERS) - in excess of the plan, which is a point in management's favour on delivery, though the FY21 spike of Rs 164 cr (14.4% of sales) accounts for half of it.

blocks.text: **Classification: asset-light today, asset-heavy tomorrow, and the transition is the risk.** On the historical record GRSE is asset-light by any measure - gross block of Rs 816 cr supporting Rs 5,071 cr of production, capex at 1.1-1.6% of sales for three years, fixed-asset turnover of 12.16x [F] (AR2025 p.38), [F] (NUMBERS). The announced programme would raise capex by roughly an order of magnitude against a revenue base whose order book is contracting. That is a materially different capital-allocation profile than the one that produced the 43% ROCE, and it is being undertaken by a company that has never built a greenfield shipyard [AI].

blocks.text: **Our read [AI].** The structural argument is sound: when 65% of cost is customer-nominated equipment ordered early at fixed prices, and the contract itself is fixed price, a mid-contract commodity move has limited effect on projects already under way. But the company's flat assertion of 'no exposure to commodity risk' is not the same statement as the rating agency's 'profitability susceptible to unprecedented input price increase', and the FY25 onerous provision demonstrates that cost overruns on fixed-price work do occur and do hit the P&L. The exposure is not to spot commodity prices on in-flight projects; it is to **bid-time cost estimation on projects not yet won**, which is precisely where the next Rs 1,50,000 cr of work would come from. Management acknowledges this: 'For all the new contracts which we are yet to sign or where we are bidding, we will factor this aspect of uncertainty also' [MC] (CALL May 2026).

blocks.text: Method [E]: the FY26 material-cost base is estimated by applying the FY25 ratio of (cost of materials consumed plus B&D purchases less change in work-in-progress inventory) to revenue - Rs 3,535 cr on Rs 5,076 cr, or 69.7% - to FY26 revenue of Rs 7,002 cr, giving Rs 4,880 cr [E] (AR2025 p.152, NUMBERS). FY26 EBITDA of Rs 795 cr and PBT of Rs 1,005 cr are as reported [F] (NUMBERS). The FY26 expense breakdown is not published in this folder, so the base is an estimate, not a disclosure. The result is a structural finding rather than a precise one: **with materials at roughly 70% of revenue and an EBITDA margin of 11.4%, a 5% unhedged input shock removes about three-tenths of EBITDA and a 10% shock removes about three-fifths.** The operating leverage runs both ways, and it is the reason the rating agency's single key weakness is the fixed-price contract structure [F] (RATING).

blocks.text: **The analyst who asked the right question did not get an answer.** On the Q4 FY26 call, Sanjeev Zarbade of Antique asked twice whether, adjusting for the provision write-backs in Q4 FY25 and Q4 FY26, sustainable margin is nearer 9.5-10% rather than 11.5%. The CMD replied, twice, only that 'we will be able to maintain similar margins in the coming year' and, when pressed on whether that meant 11.5%, 'I really can't say the exact' [MC] (CALL May 2026). The question has now been asked and deflected across two calls [AI].

**Bottom line on whether margin improvement is structural.** Part of it clearly is: an EBITDA base of Rs 795 cr on a Rs 7,002 cr revenue base cannot be explained by provision reversals alone, and fixed-cost absorption on a business that has grown 6x in six years on a broadly flat headcount is a genuine economic effect [F] (NUMBERS, AR2025 p.27). But two specific, disclosed, non-recurring items sit inside the last two years - a Rs 100 cr profit uplift from a cost-to-complete revision in FY25, flagged by the auditor as an Emphasis of Matter, and unquantified provision reversals in FY26, flagged by the rating agency. **On the evidence available, the sustainable margin cannot be distinguished from the reported margin, and the analyst estimate of 9.5-10% that management declined to reject is as defensible as 11.4% [AI].**

sections.title: Unit economics: what can and cannot be built from the disclosures

items: **No per-ship cost or margin is disclosed in any period.** Revenue is recognised over time on a cost-to-cost basis for the shipbuilding division as a whole; the accounts give a single shipbuilding contract-revenue line of Rs 4,448.53 cr for FY25 with no project split [F] (AR2025 p.178).

**No capacity is expressed in tonnage, CGT or man-hours.** Capacity is a count of concurrent platforms of unspecified size [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), so a revenue-per-unit-of-capacity calculation is not meaningful.
**No segment margins exist** because GRSE is exempted from Ind AS 108 [F] (AR2025 p.143).

**Material cost per ship cannot be derived** - cost of materials consumed is a single company-wide figure and the inventory note does not allocate by project except for one line, 'Variable items of P17A' at Rs 1,838.59 cr [F] (AR2025 p.170).
**Utilisation is not disclosed**, so a contribution-per-berth-year calculation is impossible.

subsections.title: What would have to be true for unit economics to improve

items: **Higher value-added share.** Value added fell from 59% of production (FY21) to 29% (FY25) [F] (AR2025 p.27). Reversing that requires either more in-house content per ship (indigenisation of propulsion, more deck machinery per platform) or a mix shift toward less equipment-intensive vessels. Management's indigenisation roadmap points the right way but at a five-to-ten-year pace [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**A higher-margin mix.** The lines management describes as higher margin - ship repair ('margins are high... we have not yet executed a very big order on ship repair') and the naval gun ('margins are good... there is no competition') - are together under 6% of the order book [MC] (CALL Feb 2026), [E] (CALL Aug 2026). Scaling either would move the blended margin; neither has been scaled.

**Aftermarket and spares.** Base-and-depot spares are 10-15% of project cost and are delivered after ship handover; management describes them as the FY28 cushion [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Whether they carry a higher margin than construction is not disclosed - an analyst asked precisely this in May 2026 and the answer addressed price escalation rather than margin [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**Labour cost discipline.** Employee benefits expense was Rs 360.85 cr in FY25, 7.1% of revenue, down from 9.7% in FY24 [F] (AR2025 p.180), [E]. A pay commission expected 'next year' at 15-20% would add roughly Rs 54-72 cr on the FY25 base [E], which management says is already in its projections [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Headcount has fallen from 2,834 (FY15) to 1,690 (FY25), and the strategy is explicitly to keep a lean permanent blue-collar force and outsource [F] (AR2025 p.27), [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Winning work at better prices.** Management has been explicit that some orders were taken at low or subsidised margins 'for sustenance and entry', and that order book enhancement will not now be at the cost of margin [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). That is an intention, not an economic mechanism - in a competitive fixed-price bid against four to six yards, margin is set by the second-lowest bidder [AI].

blocks.text: Everything in this section is **standalone** - GRSE has no subsidiary, joint venture or associate, so standalone and consolidated are the same thing [F] (AR2025 p.146). Our statements data covers ten fiscal years to FY26 plus twelve quarters and a trailing twelve months; full audited notes are available only to FY25, because no FY26 annual report is in this folder. FY26 balance-sheet and cash-flow detail therefore comes from summary figures in our statements data and from the credit rating report. There is **no segment reporting in any year** [F] (AR2025 p.143). Cash is not separated from other assets in our statements data, so the enterprise value used in valuation does not net off the Rs 3,511 cr cash balance [F] (NUMBERS). The report prints the full statements separately; figures are quoted here with their years rather than repeated in full.

items: **Revenue grew 6.1x in six years** - Rs 1,141 cr (FY21) to Rs 7,002 cr (FY26) - with nine-year, five-year and three-year CAGRs of 25.3%, 43.7% and 39.8% [F] (NUMBERS). None of this is organic in the usual sense: it is the S-curve of two large contracts.

**EBITDA was negative in FY17 and FY18** (-Rs 161 cr and -Rs 15 cr) and the company was still profitable at the PAT line in both years, because other income of Rs 217 cr and Rs 179 cr more than covered the operating loss [F] (NUMBERS). This is the structural signature of the business: an operating company sitting on a float [AI].

**Other income has been the swing factor for a decade.** It was 1,085% of PBT in FY17, 94% in FY19, 66% in FY23, 47% in FY25 and 27% in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). Its declining share is genuinely good news - it means operating profit is finally the main event. But the absolute amount has been remarkably stable at Rs 154-335 cr across ten years while revenue grew 7.6x, and it fell in FY26 (Rs 274 cr from Rs 335 cr) [F] (NUMBERS). In Q1 FY27 it jumped back to Rs 100 cr, 43% of the Rs 232 cr PBT [E] (NUMBERS).

**The composition of other income is disclosed only for FY25:** interest income Rs 249.74 cr (74.6%), liabilities written back Rs 32.69 cr, other items Rs 31.94 cr - of which Rs 29.56 cr was a refund of previously levied liquidated damages on an earlier delivered project - fair-value gains Rs 8.35 cr, foreign exchange gains Rs 7.72 cr and mutual fund profit Rs 2.94 cr [F] (AR2025 p.179). Interest income was Rs 246 cr in FY26 [F] (RATING).
**Tax rate has been stable at 25-28%** since FY20, consistent with the full domestic corporate rate; there is no tax-holiday or incentive distortion [F] (NUMBERS).

**Depreciation is trivially small** - Rs 49 cr in FY26 on Rs 7,002 cr of revenue, 0.7% - reflecting the asset-light structure and the fully-depreciated state of much of the Kolkata plant [F] (NUMBERS).

**Finance cost of Rs 16 cr in FY26** includes items that are not interest on debt: in FY25 the Rs 10.32 cr total comprised Rs 2.97 cr of bank overdraft interest, Rs 6.18 cr of interest on liquidated-damages liability, Rs 0.80 cr of lease unwinding and Rs 0.38 cr of MSME interest [F] (AR2025 p.180). The single largest component was a contract-penalty accrual, not borrowing cost [AI].

**The balance sheet is 66% customer money.** Contract liabilities were Rs 6,900.04 cr at 31 Mar 2025 against total assets of Rs 10,354.23 cr and equity of Rs 2,079.26 cr [F] (AR2025 p.151, p.177). Contract liabilities fell Rs 427 cr year on year while revenue rose 41% - the float is draining [E].

**Cash and bank was Rs 3,731.85 cr at 31 Mar 2025** - 36% of total assets - of which only Rs 3.88 cr sits in cash and cash equivalents and Rs 3,727.97 cr in bank deposits with three-to-twelve-month maturities, including Rs 89.99 cr earmarked for P-17A variable items [F] (AR2025 p.151, p.172). It fell to Rs 3,511 cr by 31 Mar 2026 [F] (RATING).

**Inventories were Rs 3,552.25 cr, 34% of total assets**, of which Rs 1,838.59 cr is a single line, 'Variable items of P17A', and Rs 357.43 cr lies with third parties [F] (AR2025 p.170). The provision for obsolescence is Rs 8.26 cr - 0.24% of inventory - and was reduced from Rs 11.06 cr during FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.170). Inventory fell Rs 432 cr in FY25, the single largest positive working-capital movement in the cash flow [F] (AR2025 p.153).

**Other current assets of Rs 1,775.67 cr (17% of assets) are dominated by two items:** a GST receivable of Rs 1,191.00 cr and advances to suppliers of Rs 539.55 cr, both of which grew sharply (GST up Rs 264.58 cr, supplier advances up Rs 200.91 cr) [F] (AR2025 p.172). A Rs 1,191 cr GST balance is 2.3x the year's profit after tax and deserves a direct question to management on recoverability and timing [AI].

**Trade receivables are small but the ageing deteriorated.** Rs 259.46 cr at 31 Mar 2025 from Rs 194.21 cr, with the 6-12 month bucket rising from Rs 9.38 cr to Rs 94.96 cr - a tenfold increase [F] (AR2025 p.171). Debtor days then jumped from 19 (FY25) to 64 (FY26), against a prior three-year average of about 15 [F] (NUMBERS) - a rule-based amber flag in our statements data.

**Hard assets are only 5% of the balance sheet.** Property, plant and equipment Rs 490.26 cr, right-of-use assets Rs 9.19 cr, CWIP Rs 21.23 cr, intangibles Rs 15.71 cr and intangibles under development Rs 6.77 cr - Rs 543.16 cr in total [E] (AR2025 p.151).
**There is essentially no goodwill and no acquired intangible.** Intangibles of Rs 22.48 cr including work in progress are 0.2% of assets [E] (AR2025 p.151). No acquisition has ever been made.

**Financial debt is negligible in every year.** Borrowings were nil at 31 Mar 2025 (Rs 55.58 cr a year earlier, repaid), and Rs 37 cr at 31 Mar 2026, which the rating agency identifies as lease liabilities rather than bank debt [F] (AR2025 p.151), [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING).

items: **The volatility is not noise; it is the order cycle.** CFO of +Rs 1,450 cr in FY23 coincided with the order book peaking above Rs 20,000 cr; CFO of -Rs 707 cr (FY24) and -Rs 290 cr (FY26) coincided with the book draining. In this business, operating cash flow is a first derivative of the order book, not of profit [AI].

**The FY25 cash flow shows the mechanism precisely.** Operating profit before working capital changes was Rs 460.75 cr. Working capital then absorbed Rs 269.28 cr, made up of inventory releasing Rs 432.19 cr and trade payables adding Rs 168.75 cr, against other current assets absorbing Rs 451.38 cr and other current liabilities (principally contract liabilities) absorbing Rs 425.39 cr. After Rs 175.89 cr of tax, CFO was Rs 15.59 cr against PAT of Rs 527.40 cr [F] (AR2025 p.153).

**Interest income is classified in investing, which flatters investing and depresses operating.** Rs 249.74 cr of interest received sits in cash flow from investing in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.153). Even adding it back, adjusted operating cash of about Rs 265 cr is half of reported PAT [E].

**Financing outflow is almost entirely dividend.** FY25: Rs 118.02 cr of dividends against Rs 186.75 cr of total financing outflow; the balance was Rs 54.40 cr of overdraft repayment and Rs 13.33 cr of interest and lease payments [F] (AR2025 p.154).

**Free cash flow was negative in four of the last five years**, cumulatively -Rs 176 cr over five years and -Rs 1,173 cr over three [F] (NUMBERS) - an amber rule-based flag. Dividends of Rs 158.65 cr (FY25) were therefore paid out of the cash pile, not out of the year's free cash flow [AI].

**Closing cash and cash equivalents were Rs 3.88 cr at 31 Mar 2025** [F] (AR2025 p.154). The Rs 3,727.97 cr of bank deposits sits outside the cash-flow statement's definition of cash, which is why the statement shows a net decrease of only Rs 1.39 cr on a year in which the deposit balance moved [F] (AR2025 p.153-154). Readers who look only at the cash-flow statement will materially misread the liquidity position [AI].

sections.title: Working capital: the headline number is the least informative number

blocks.text: GRSE's working capital days are **negative** - minus 80 days in FY26, minus 169 in FY25, minus 1,012 at the FY21 extreme [F] (NUMBERS). Read naively this says the business is funded by its suppliers and customers and needs no capital. Read correctly it says something quite different: the negative balance is customer stage payments received in advance of revenue recognition, and its size is a direct function of **how much unexecuted order book the company is sitting on**. When the order book grows, advances arrive and working capital goes more negative. When the order book runs off, the advances are consumed by revenue recognition and working capital converges toward zero - which is exactly what has happened, from minus 1,012 days to minus 80 days over five years [AI] (NUMBERS).

The convergence toward zero is the single most important trend in the accounts. It simultaneously explains negative operating cash flow, the Rs 221 cr fall in the cash balance over FY26, and why other income (interest on the float) will be structurally lower in future unless the order book is replenished [AI] (NUMBERS, RATING).

subsections.title: What drove the change, and the cash consequence

items: **Inventory release (positive).** Inventories fell Rs 432.19 cr in FY25, releasing cash [F] (AR2025 p.153). Within this, raw materials and equipment fell from Rs 2,176.61 cr to Rs 1,587.12 cr while 'Variable items of P17A' rose from Rs 1,701.71 cr to Rs 1,838.59 cr [F] (AR2025 p.170) - consumption of general procurement offset by continued accumulation on the frigate programme.

**Contract liabilities draining (negative).** Other current liabilities fell Rs 425.39 cr in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.153); contract liabilities specifically fell from Rs 7,327.17 cr to Rs 6,900.04 cr [F] (AR2025 p.177). This is the mechanical consequence of recognising Rs 5,076 cr of revenue against a shrinking order book [AI].

**Other current assets absorbing (negative).** Up Rs 451.38 cr in FY25, of which a Rs 264.58 cr increase in the GST receivable (to Rs 1,191.00 cr) and a Rs 200.91 cr increase in advances to suppliers (to Rs 539.55 cr) [F] (AR2025 p.153, p.172). No management explanation is offered for either in any document [AI].

**Debtor days (negative, FY26).** From 19 to 64 days [F] (NUMBERS) - an amber rule-based flag. The FY25 ageing already showed the 6-12 month bucket rising from Rs 9.38 cr to Rs 94.96 cr [F] (AR2025 p.171). Management has not been asked about receivables on any of the four calls in this folder [AI].

**Management's own explanation of working capital.** There is none. On no call in this folder does management discuss working capital, cash conversion or the negative operating cash flow. The nearest statements are the description of stage payments ('I don't get any advance. I get a stage payment') and the disclosure of a Rs 3,009 cr cash balance split between own funds and project funds [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Nov 2025). **No analyst on any of the four calls asked why operating cash flow was negative in a record profit year [AI].**

blocks.text: **Cash conversion consequence.** Over FY24-FY26 GRSE reported Rs 1,632 cr of profit after tax and generated -Rs 981 cr of operating cash [F] (NUMBERS). The Rs 2,613 cr gap is essentially the unwinding of the customer float plus the build-up of GST and supplier advances. Cash and bank fell from Rs 3,732 cr to Rs 3,511 cr over FY26 while Rs 223 cr left in financing (principally dividends) [F] (RATING, NUMBERS). The company remains very liquid - but it is being liquid out of a stock, not out of a flow [AI].

**Covenant and bank-limit implications.** GRSE has sanctioned fund-based limits of Rs 227.00 cr and non-fund-based limits of Rs 8,566.00 cr under a multiple banking arrangement, secured by hypothecation of the entire current assets excluding fixed deposits [F] (AR2025 p.198). The rating agency reaffirmed CARE AAA/Stable and CARE A1+ on 22 Jun 2026 and enhanced the long-term/short-term facility from Rs 7,361 cr to Rs 12,958 cr, assigning a further Rs 300 cr short-term facility [F] (RATING). No financial covenants are disclosed; the rating report states 'Assumptions/Covenants: Not applicable' [F] (RATING). The rating agency's own negative triggers are the closest thing to a covenant: a substantial decline in GoI stake, a significant continuous decline in order book **and** PBILDT margin, a policy change increasing competition, or liquid funds falling below Rs 3,000 cr on a continued basis [F] (RATING). Two of those five - order book decline and the liquidity floor - are live [AI]. The auditor confirms quarterly stock and book-debt returns filed with banks agree with the books [F] (AR2025 p.145).

blocks.text: **The bank guarantees are the real leverage in this business.** Rs 6,443 cr of bank guarantees at 31 Mar 2025 against Rs 2,079 cr of equity - 3.1x - is what supports the customer stage payments that fund the balance sheet. The rating agency explicitly reclassifies these as working-capital debt, producing an 'overall gearing' of 2.42x (FY25) and 1.98x (FY26), against the financial debt-to-equity of 0.00-0.01x in our statements data [F] (RATING, NUMBERS). Neither figure alone describes the company. The guarantees are performance-backed and covered by cash of Rs 3,511 cr plus a Rs 8,566 cr sanctioned non-fund-based limit [F] (AR2025 p.198), [F] (RATING), so this is not a solvency concern - but anyone describing GRSE as 'debt-free' should know that the off-balance-sheet obligation is three times equity [AI].

items: **Related-party leases.** The land lease (Rs 6.56 cr liability, Rs 0.55 cr annual rent) is from the Kolkata Port Trust / Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, a government entity [F] (AR2025 p.197), [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). The three-plus Khidderpore dry docks are under a separate concession agreement with the same lessor [F] (AR2025 p.81). SMPK is simultaneously GRSE's landlord and, since Aug 2026, a customer for an electric tug [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Because both are government entities, neither the lease terms nor the tug contract falls within the detailed related-party disclosure GRSE publishes [AI].

**Promoter-group guarantees.** None disclosed. The Government of India does not guarantee GRSE's obligations; the rating agency's analytical approach is 'Standalone, while factoring linkages with the parent, GoI' [F] (RATING).

**Off-balance-sheet items.** Beyond guarantees and indemnity bonds, none disclosed. The auditor confirms no benami proceedings, no wilful defaulter status, no undisclosed income surrendered in tax assessments, no non-cash transactions with directors, and no funds advanced to or received from intermediaries [F] (AR2025 p.145-146).

**Title deeds.** All immovable property is held in the company's name except one building of Rs 95.96 lakh carrying value, jointly owned one-third each with Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders and Goa Shipyard since 15 Jun 1998 [F] (AR2025 p.199).

blocks.text: **Overall assessment [AI].** High quality on the traditional tests - no goodwill, no acquired intangibles, no debt, no pledges, no benami or title issues, clean auditor CARO, and a very large liquid buffer. The quality question is not about solvency; it is about **composition and direction**. More than half the asset base is working capital whose value depends on contracts being completed profitably, a third is deposits funded by customer advances that are draining, and 5% is the actual shipyard. A Rs 1,191 cr GST receivable, a Rs 540 cr supplier-advance balance, an inventory obsolescence provision of 0.24% and debtor days quadrupling in a year are all individually defensible and collectively worth a direct conversation with management.

subsections.title: Emphasis of Matter - the most important accounting disclosure in the file

blocks.text: **FY25 carried an Emphasis of Matter.** 'We draw attention to note 48 of the financial statements, which describes the effects of change in estimation of cost to complete in respect of projects P17A and NGOPV. Our opinion is not modified in respect of this matter' [F] (AR2025 p.141). Note 48 reads: 'Considering the advancement in construction stage of ongoing projects (i.e., P17A, NGOPV), cost to completion of these projects have been reviewed on the basis of management's best available estimates and revised accordingly. Due to such revisions, cost to completion is reduced by Rs 43,303 Lakh and Profits for the current Year is increased by an amount of Rs 10,000 Lakh' [F] (AR2025 p.199). **That is Rs 433.03 cr of estimated cost removed and Rs 100 cr of profit added - about 19% of FY25 profit after tax and 24% of FY25 EBITDA [E].**

This is not an accounting irregularity. Cost-to-complete revision is intrinsic to percentage-of-completion accounting, the revision is in the direction you would expect as a project de-risks, the auditor tested it as a Key Audit Matter and flagged it transparently, and both the auditor and the C&AG signed off without qualification [F] (AR2025 p.141, p.101). But three things follow for an investor [AI]. First, a round Rs 100 cr of the FY25 profit uplift came from a management estimate, not from cash or from a transaction. Second, the same mechanism could reverse: if costs to complete are later revised upward, profit is reduced. Third, and most relevant now, the rating agency states that the FY26 margin also benefited from 'reversal of excess cost provisions created in earlier years' without quantifying it [F] (RATING), and the FY26 annual report is not available in this folder to test that statement. **Two consecutive years of margin expansion carry a disclosed but incompletely quantified estimate-revision component.**

subsections.title: CARO, compliance and the remaining checks

items: **CARO 2020 - clean across all twenty-one clauses.** Proper fixed-asset and intangible records; three-year physical verification cycle; title deeds in the company's name (one jointly held building excepted); no revaluation; no benami proceedings; inventory physically verified with no class discrepancy above 10%; quarterly bank returns agree with the books; no loans or guarantees given; no deposits accepted; cost records maintained; statutory dues generally regular with none outstanding over six months; no undisclosed income; no default on borrowings; not a wilful defaulter; short-term funds not used for long-term purposes; no IPO or preferential allotment; **no fraud noticed or reported and no ADT-4 filed**; no whistle-blower complaints received during the year; related-party transactions compliant with sections 177 and 188; internal audit system commensurate with size; no non-cash transactions with directors; no cash losses in FY25 or FY24; no auditor resignation; no material uncertainty on meeting liabilities within twelve months; no unspent CSR [F] (AR2025 p.145-147).

**Audit trail.** 'The Company has in place an accounting software for maintaining its books of account which has a feature of recording audit trail (edit log) facility and the same has operated throughout the year for all relevant transactions... we did not come across any instance of audit trail feature being tampered with. Additionally, the audit trail is preserved by the Company as per the statutory requirements for record retention' [F] (AR2025 p.144). All accounting transactions are processed through SAP with no processing outside the IT system, per the C&AG directions response [F] (AR2025 p.148).
**Restatements.** None. The statement of changes in equity shows no changes in equity share capital due to prior-period errors [F] (AR2025 p.155).

**Common control or unusual accounting.** None identified. There are no subsidiaries, no acquisitions, no common-control transactions, no ESOPs ('no Stock Options were issued by the Company to Whole-time Directors') and no share buyback or capital restructuring [F] (AR2025 p.96, p.146).

**Onerous contracts.** Rs 11.97 cr of additional onerous provision was recognised in FY25 for the Bangladesh boats 'due to Cost/time overrun', on top of Rs 2.71 cr carried forward; all of it was utilised during the year, leaving nil at 31 Mar 2025 [F] (AR2025 p.178). The auditor's Rule 11 paragraph flags 'Guarantee Repair and Onerous Contract' as the only long-term contracts with material foreseeable losses, adequately provided [F] (AR2025 p.143).

**Disputed statutory dues.** Rs 22.44 cr not deposited at 31 Mar 2025: VAT Rs 5.07 cr (2007-08, WB Taxation Tribunal), income tax Rs 16.25 cr (AY 2008-09 and 2016-17, CIT Appeals) and GST Rs 1.04 cr (2017-18) [F] (AR2025 p.146). Old and small relative to the balance sheet [AI].

blocks.text: **What the documents do not cover.** (1) **No segment reporting in any year** - the auditor expressly states the financial statements comply with the standards 'except disclosure under Ind AS 108 Operating Segments' under the defence-production exemption [F] (AR2025 p.143). (2) **No detailed related-party disclosure** - the Ind AS 24 government-entity exemption is availed, so the Navy relationship is invisible in the RPT note [F] (AR2025 p.189). (3) **No FY26 audited accounts are in this folder**, so FY26's provision reversals, contingent liabilities, inventory ageing, receivable ageing, cash-flow detail and any FY26 Emphasis of Matter cannot be examined. (4) **No customer concentration disclosure** in any year. (5) **No capacity utilisation disclosure** in any year. (6) **The C&AG comments page is blank in the extracted text**; the corporate governance section states comments were Nil, but the primary document could not be read [F] (AR2025 p.150, p.101).

**Overall accounting-quality assessment [AI]: high on process, constrained on disclosure, with one identified earnings-estimate sensitivity.** Twenty years without an audit qualification, nil C&AG comments, a functioning SAP audit trail, a clean CARO, no fraud, no restatements and no related-party complexity are a genuinely strong record and better than most listed Indian industrials. The offsetting facts are that the two largest P&L judgements - contract stage of completion and inventory valuation - are both Key Audit Matters, that a Rs 100 cr estimate revision was material to FY25 profit and was flagged by an Emphasis of Matter, that FY26 carried further unquantified provision reversals per the rating agency, and that the two disclosures an outside analyst most needs - segments and customer concentration - are legally exempted. We would rate the **accounting** high and the **disclosure** low, and they are different things.

blocks.text: **Economic substance versus headline size.** The headline related-party disclosure is small: Rs 931 cr of sales and Rs 3.43 cr of KMP pay. items: **Promoter holding has been unchanged at 74.50% for all twelve quarters** in our shareholding data; the one-year change is exactly zero [F] (NUMBERS). This is the statutory maximum-stability case: the Government of India has neither bought nor sold, and there is no disclosed disinvestment plan in any document.
**No pledges.** None disclosed anywhere; the promoter is the President of India and the shares are described as 'not actively traded' [F] (AR2025 p.103).

**Institutional ownership is strikingly thin for a Rs 26,803 cr market capitalisation.** FIIs 3.21% and DIIs 1.93% at Jun 2026 - together 5.14% [F] (NUMBERS). Domestic institutions have more than halved their holding since Mar 2024 (6.14% to 1.93%), a cut of about two-thirds over nine quarters [E] (NUMBERS). At 31 Mar 2025 the institutional register comprised 16 mutual funds holding 1.64%, 78 foreign portfolio investors holding 3.84%, 9 insurance companies holding 0.04% and 3 AIFs holding 0.22% [F] (AR2025 p.103). No bank or financial institution held a single share [F] (AR2025 p.103).

**The retail base exploded and is now shrinking.** Shareholder count rose from 108,922 (Sep 2023) to a peak of 425,900 (Sep 2025) and has fallen for three consecutive quarters to 399,380 (Jun 2026) - a net loss of about 26,500 shareholders [E] (NUMBERS). At 31 Mar 2025, 409,420 shareholders (98.9% of the register) held 12.49% of the equity, while 131 holders held 82.19% [F] (AR2025 p.103). There are no stock options: 'no Stock Options were issued by the Company to Whole-time Directors' [F] (AR2025 p.96). subsections.title: What the competitive structure actually looks like

items: **The field has widened, and management says so plainly.** 'There was a time when, before we were listed, of course, we used to take the system for granted that orders used to come aplenty on nomination. Now every order, every, I repeat, every order is on competition, except what we work and get from the foreign clients. And today, the field has expanded' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The company's own SWOT lists as threats: 'Competition from Private and Public Shipyards' and 'Emerging private sector firms in the Indian shipbuilding industry and their impact on the Indian Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding/ship repair market' [F] (AR2025 p.82).

**Programme splitting caps any single win.** The P-17 Bravo will go 4 ships to L1 and 3 to L2; the MCMV 8 and 4; the LPD 2 and 2; the 120 fast interceptor craft 80 and 40 [MC] (CALL May 2026). Even a clean sweep on every named programme leaves the majority of the Rs 1,50,000 cr with someone else [AI].

**Barriers differ sharply by segment.** For frontline warships the field is four to six yards and the barrier is qualification, security clearance and design experience [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). For large commercial vessels GRSE is on the wrong side of the barrier - it cannot physically bid the LPD, VLGC or container-ship tenders alone and must partner [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Aug 2026). For engineering products, the AR names 'competition for Engineering Products from small players' [F] (AR2025 p.82).

**GRSE competes with entities that share its controlling shareholder and, in one case, its nominee director.** The Government Nominee Director on GRSE's board simultaneously sits on the boards of Mazagon Dock and Hindustan Shipyard [F] (AR2025 p.33). Programme allocation between these yards is a decision taken inside the same ministry that appoints all their boards. Whether that is a risk or a protection depends entirely on the ministry's allocation preference in any given cycle, and it is not something an outside shareholder can underwrite [AI].

**Alliances cut across the competitive lines.** GRSE and HSL are consortium partners on the LPD while both are rivals on other programmes; Swan has an MoU with MDL for the same LPD [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). GRSE also outsources whole platforms to a large private yard under a PPP model [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The boundary between competitor, partner and subcontractor is fluid.

blocks.text: **Competitive landscape assessment [AI].** GRSE occupies a defensible position in a narrow segment (frontline warships up to 10,000 t, research vessels, and a niche 30 mm naval gun) and a weak position everywhere else. The defensible segment is being allocated by tender among a widening field of four to six credible bidders, with deliberate two-way splits that cap upside, and with an allocating authority that owns all the bidders. The weak segments - large commercial vessels, ship repair at scale, autonomous platforms - are exactly where the growth narrative sits and where GRSE currently needs a partner, a foreign designer or a yard it has not yet built. Peer financials are not disclosed, so no relative-performance judgement can be evidenced; the comparison that can be made is that GRSE's own return on capital of 43% is unusually high for a fixed-price government contractor, which is itself a reason to ask how durable it is.

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **1. Does the qualification barrier translate into pricing power, or only into access?** The evidence says access only. Every contract is fixed price, negotiated once with a monopsony buyer; management describes the process as price negotiation on an L1 bid and says explicitly that some orders were taken 'at very low margins... for sustenance and entry' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026). A nine-out-of-ten regulatory barrier that produces an 11% EBITDA margin is telling you that the barrier protects the right to compete, not the right to price. The board notes in this dashboard reach the same conclusion from a different direction - 'effectively none; naval contracts are negotiated with a single buyer on cost-plus or fixed-price terms' [AI] (BOARD).

**2. Does any of the moat survive the move into commercial shipbuilding?** Almost none of it does. The regulatory barrier is irrelevant to a German shipowner. The 65-year Navy relationship is irrelevant to ONGC's tender committee. The design IP is insufficient for VLGCs and container ships, where GRSE must partner a proven foreign builder [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Management's own expected win rate in commercial is 15% against 20% in defence, in a field it describes as much larger [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). The growth story is therefore being told about the segment where the moat does not apply [AI].

blocks.text: **Overall moat conclusion [AI].** GRSE has a narrow, genuine, and durable moat - the right to be one of four to six entities the Indian state will place a warship order with. That moat is regulatory, it is granted rather than earned, and it protects volume and survival rather than price. It scores highly on the one factor that matters for existence and poorly on every factor that matters for economics: no input control, no network effect, no pricing power, limited technology differentiation and a physical footprint that management is spending Rs 4,400 cr to escape. A 5.1 average is the right shape of answer: this is a protected franchise, not a compounding one.

subsections.title: Why TAM cannot be translated into company revenue

blocks.text: **Illustrative share arithmetic, labelled as illustration only [E].** The MD&A states Indian defence shipbuilding is worth more than Rs 1.5 lakh crore over the next decade - about Rs 15,000 cr a year across the whole industry [F] (AR2025 p.80), [E]. GRSE's FY26 revenue was Rs 7,002 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Taken at face value, GRSE would already hold 47% of the entire national defence shipbuilding market [E] - which is obviously not true, and demonstrates the point: **the TAM figure and the revenue figure are not on the same basis.** The TAM is almost certainly an order-value figure for new acquisitions, spread over multi-year build cycles and excluding follow-on spares, refits and the non-defence work that is a quarter of GRSE's book. Any calculation that multiplies a TAM by an assumed market share to produce a revenue forecast is meaningless here [AI].

A second illustration, on management's own numbers [E]. Management quotes an AoN-accorded pipeline of about Rs 1,50,000 cr and an expected win rate of 'at least 20%' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Aug 2026). Twenty percent of Rs 1,50,000 cr is Rs 30,000 cr of order value. Management also states that a project of NGC scale takes eight years to complete and that revenue recognition follows an S-curve starting in year two [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Rs 30,000 cr spread over eight years averages **about Rs 3,750 cr of annual revenue [E]** - half of GRSE's current run rate. This is not a forecast; it is an arithmetic demonstration that even a successful outcome on management's own assumptions does not, by itself, sustain the current revenue level. Sustaining it requires either a higher win rate, a larger pipeline, faster execution, or the commercial business scaling [AI].
