Its purpose is to show the shape of the problem: **on contracted work plus the single most likely addition, GRSE has roughly Rs 5,800 cr a year of average revenue against a Rs 7,500 cr run rate.** Everything above that has to be won in competition [AI].

items: **Extreme supply-side concentration in defence.** Five public sector shipyards (GRSE, MDL, GSL, Cochin, HSL) plus L&T, with Swan, Shoft, Chowgule and Titagarh at the margin - management's count for the Rs 1,40,000-1,50,000 cr of contenders is 'just about five to six shipyards' [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL Feb 2026). The AR describes the five PSU yards as 'the frontrunners in the defence shipbuilding space' with private yards 'repositioning themselves as capable warship builders' [F] (AR2025 p.80).

**Extreme demand-side concentration.** One buyer (the Ministry of Defence, via the Navy and Coast Guard) for roughly three-quarters of the book; a handful of other ministries and state agencies for most of the rest [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Channel structure: direct, tendered, no intermediaries.** Defence work is sold through the Defence Acquisition Procedure - AoN, RFP, bid, L1, price negotiation, contract, 15-stage payment [MC] (CALL May 2026). Non-defence PSU work now runs through demand aggregation by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). Commercial export work is direct owner-to-yard negotiation, where management says the binding constraint is relationship formation rather than contracting - 'it is just a question of making the break' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Engineering products go to the Indian Army, BRO, NHIDCL and state PWDs under MoUs, and Rs 1,599.06 cr of procurement ran through the Government e-Marketplace in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.44, p.49).

**Vendor-side concentration.** Bharat Electronics dominates the electronics content; HAL routes marine gas turbines; propulsion engines remain import-dependent [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). On the other side, 73.9% of GRSE's procurement value went to micro and small enterprises in FY25 - a wide supplier base for everything except the expensive part [F] (AR2025 p.48).

**The structural asymmetry [AI]:** concentrated buyers, concentrated critical suppliers, and a fragmented base of small vendors in between. GRSE holds the weakest bargaining position of the three at both ends of its own value chain.

blocks.text: **The supported themes are real but slow; the unsupported themes are the ones doing the work in the narrative [AI].** Indigenisation, naval fleet expansion and policy support are genuine, documented and long-dated - they set a floor under GRSE's existence and a ceiling on how quickly it can grow, because they operate on DAC and RFP timelines that management itself measures in years. The themes that would justify a re-rating - autonomous warfare, defence exports, scaled commercial shipbuilding, structural margin expansion, a bigger yard - are each at prototype, letter-of-intent, aspiration or construction-drawing stage. Not one of them has produced a contract. An investor underwriting GRSE today is underwriting the supported themes at the supported pace, and buying the unsupported themes as a free option - except that at the current price the option does not appear to be free [AI].

**The order book guidance was the largest miss and has never been acknowledged.** Rs 50,000 cr guided, Rs 15,324 cr delivered. Neither the May 2026 nor the Aug 2026 call contains an acknowledgement, an explanation of the variance, or a question from any analyst about it [MC] (CALL May 2026, CALL Aug 2026). Instead the framing was inverted: the falling order book was presented as evidence of execution quality [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). **That inversion is the single most important behavioural signal in the transcripts [AI].**

**Margin guidance is systematically vague.** 'Similar margins' has now been offered for FY27, FY28 and FY29 without a number, and a direct question about adjusting for provision write-backs was deflected twice in one exchange [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**There is no negative guidance anywhere.** Across four calls covering 21 months, management never guides down, never quantifies a risk and never assigns a probability below confidence. The nearest thing to a caution is 'the order book deficit currently is there' and 'the deficit or the gap at this moment is not a grave concern' [MC] (CALL May 2026). Analysts, to their credit, raised the gap question on three of four calls [MC] (CALL Nov 2025, CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026).

**Operational disclosure quality is genuinely high.** Physical progress percentages ship by ship, order book line by line, vendor workshare, indigenisation by component category, payment-stage mechanics and revenue-recognition S-curve explanations are all volunteered in detail. This is far above the norm for an Indian PSU, and it is the reason the guidance misses can be identified at all [AI].

**Over nine years GRSE has reported Rs 2,568 cr of profit and generated Rs 1,070 cr of operating cash - a cumulative conversion of 0.42x.** Over the last three years, which include every record result, the conversion is negative. This is the single hardest fact in the file to argue away, and it has never been raised by any analyst on any of the four calls in this folder [AI].

**The mitigating reading, stated fairly [AI].** GRSE's cash flow is dominated by the customer float, not by receivables quality. Operating cash flow is strongly positive when the order book grows (FY20, FY21, FY23) and strongly negative when it shrinks (FY22, FY24, FY26). Interest received of Rs 249.74 cr in FY25 is classified in investing rather than operating, understating CFO; adding it back still leaves adjusted operating cash at about half of profit [F] (AR2025 p.153), [E]. And the company holds Rs 3,511 cr of cash with no debt, so no liquidity question arises today [F] (RATING). **The correct conclusion is not that earnings are fictitious - they are audited, tax is paid at 25-26%, and Rs 85.70 cr went to the exchequer in FY25 [F] (AR2025 p.39), [F] (NUMBERS). It is that earnings and cash are driven by different variables, and the variable driving cash (order book direction) is currently pointing the wrong way.**

blocks.text: **Two structural observations [AI].** First, the trend in other income dependence is genuinely improving - from 62% of PBT in FY24 to 27% in FY26 - because operating profit grew, not because other income fell much. That is the right kind of improvement. But the absolute amount of other income has been between Rs 154 cr and Rs 335 cr for ten straight years while revenue grew 7.6x [F] (NUMBERS), and it is earned on a deposit balance that is itself customer money. As contract liabilities drain from Rs 7,327 cr toward the level implied by a Rs 13,596 cr order book, the interest line has to fall [AI]. Second, Q1 FY27 reversed the trend: other income of Rs 100 cr was 43% of the Rs 232 cr pre-tax profit - the highest quarterly share in two years [E] (NUMBERS).

**Net earnings-quality conclusion [AI].** The reported numbers are audited, unqualified, C&AG-reviewed, fully taxed and free of the usual manipulations - no capitalised costs of consequence, no ESOP add-backs, no acquisition accounting, no related-party revenue of significance, no goodwill. But three things separate reported profit from economic profit here: (1) a quarter to two-fifths of pre-tax profit is interest earned on customer advances that are structurally shrinking; (2) a disclosed Rs 100 cr of FY25 profit and an undisclosed amount of FY26 margin came from revisions to management estimates of cost to complete; and (3) over three years the business converted -0.60x of reported profit into operating cash. **We would characterise earnings quality as clean in process and low in cash backing** - a combination that is entirely explicable by the order-book cycle, and precisely for that reason is a warning about what the next stage of the cycle looks like.

The forecast below is **taken entirely from our DCF model** and is not our own construction. The method is a five-year free cash flow to firm build: EBITDA less tax on EBIT, less capex, less the change in net working capital; sales growth fades linearly from a starting rate to a year-five rate; a Gordon growth terminal value is added; and equity value equals enterprise value less borrowings [F] (NUMBERS). We interpret these outputs below; we do not produce alternatives.

items: **Revenue = order book conversion rate x order book, plus new intake.** Conversion is governed by the physical S-curve of each project - design phase 5-10% of project cost, hull construction to 20-25%, then a steep equipment-integration phase, then outfitting [MC] (CALL Aug 2026). GRSE's two largest projects are at 85% and 65-91% and both complete in FY27 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**Order intake = pipeline x win rate x split factor.** Pipeline is about Rs 1,50,000 cr of AoN-accorded defence projects plus roughly Rs 1 lakh crore of aggregated commercial demand [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Aug 2026). Management's own win-rate assumptions are 20% (defence) and 15% (commercial) [MC] (CALL Feb 2026). Split factors cap any single win at 4 of 7 ships (P-17B), 8 of 12 (MCMV), 2 of 4 (LPD) [MC] (CALL May 2026).

**EBITDA margin = contract price less realised cost, plus or minus estimate revisions.** All contracts are fixed price; roughly 65% of cost is customer-nominated equipment ordered early; cost-to-complete estimates are revised periodically and moved FY25 profit by Rs 100 cr [MC] (CALL Feb 2026), [F] (AR2025 p.199).

**Other income = deposit balance x rate.** Interest income was Rs 246-271 cr in each of the last three years, earned on a deposit balance funded by customer stage payments; the balance fell from Rs 3,732 cr to Rs 3,511 cr over FY26 [F] (AR2025 p.179), [F] (RATING).

**Operating cash flow = profit plus or minus the change in the customer float.** Cash flow is strongly positive when the order book grows and negative when it shrinks; the correlation is visible in every year of our statements data [F] (NUMBERS).

**Capex = maintenance plus the expansion programme.** Maintenance has run at Rs 42-77 cr a year; the announced expansion is roughly Rs 4,400 cr per management or Rs 500-600 cr over two years per the rating agency [F] (NUMBERS), [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [F] (RATING).

subsections.title: What the forecast deliberately does not assume

items: **It does not model the NGC contract.** The model starts from trailing revenue and applies a fade; it contains no explicit assumption about whether the Rs 33,000 cr contract is signed, or when it begins contributing [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING).

**It does not model the FY28 execution gap** that management itself has acknowledged - two large projects completing in FY27, NGC revenue only from FY28 and material only from FY29 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL May 2026). The linear fade from 30% to 10% smooths over a discontinuity management has described.

**It assumes zero working-capital investment** (working capital days set to 0), whereas the company actually runs at minus 80 working-capital days converging toward zero, and produced -Rs 290 cr of operating cash flow in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). A model that assumed the float continues to drain would produce lower free cash flow than shown.

**It does not credit the greenfield capacity, the Rs 69,725 cr policy package, or any subsidy.** Nor does it charge the Rs 4,400 cr of expansion capex management has described - the capex rule is mechanical, at depreciation plus new sales divided by a 9.86x fixed-asset turnover [F] (NUMBERS), [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).
**It does not model the pay commission** that management expects next year at a 15-20% increase in employee cost [MC] (CALL Aug 2026).

**It does not net off cash.** Enterprise value is market capitalisation plus borrowings, with no deduction for the Rs 3,511 cr cash balance, because our statements data does not split cash out of other assets [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING).

The bear case's 4% EBITDA margin has not been seen since FY22-FY23 and looks harsh given the current fixed-cost absorption; the bull case's 43.5% starting growth would require the order book to be replaced and converted faster than the S-curve mechanics management has described allow, in a year when net order intake has been approximately nil. subsections.title: Multiples against the disclosed peer set

blocks.text: **No peer multiples can be presented, because none are disclosed.** GRSE publishes no peer comparison; the rating report, annual report, profile and all four earnings calls contain no competitor revenue, margin, return on net worth or price-earnings figure. The competitors are named - Mazagon Dock, Goa Shipyard, Cochin Shipyard, Hindustan Shipyard, L&T Shipbuilding, Swan Defence, Shoft, Chowgule, Titagarh [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL Nov 2025), [F] (AR2025 p.80) - but no financial data for any of them appears in any source in this folder. A relative-valuation table would require inventing figures, and we will not. Listed comparables are therefore context only, and we have none to offer with evidence.

What can be said on the company's own numbers [E] (NUMBERS): at 10.22x book with a 31.8% return on equity, the market is capitalising GRSE's returns at an implied earnings yield of about 3.0%. At 32.2x EV/EBITDA on a business whose three-year operating cash conversion is -0.60x of profit, the multiple is being paid on an earnings stream that has not converted to cash. And at 3.58x EV/sales on a fixed-price contractor whose stated sustainable PAT margin in conventional shipbuilding is 'around 7.5 percentage' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), the sales multiple implies a permanent margin well above the one management is willing to name.

subsections.title: Interpreting the DCF and its assumptions

items: **The discount rate looks high for this company, and it barely matters.** A 15% WACC built on a 7% risk-free rate, a 7% equity risk premium and a 1.15 beta is a full-risk equity cost for a company that is 74.5% owned by the Government of India, rated CARE AAA, carries essentially no debt and holds Rs 3,511 cr of cash [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING). A case can be made for a lower rate. The sensitivity grid answers it: even at 13.5% with 6.5% terminal growth, fair value is Rs 784.5 - still 66.5% below the price [E] (NUMBERS).

**The margin assumption is conservative, and the model says so.** The base case uses an 8.0% EBITDA margin against 11.4% achieved in FY26 and 11.1% trailing [F] (NUMBERS). The bull case uses 10.0%, which is still below the achieved level. If a reader believes the FY26 margin is the durable one, the bull case is the relevant scenario - and it produces Rs 1,032.0, or 55.9% below the price [F] (NUMBERS). **Fixing the margin assumption does not close the gap.**

**The growth assumption is generous, not conservative.** A 30% starting growth rate applied to a company whose order book has not been replenished in five quarters, and whose two largest projects both complete in year one, is a strong assumption in GRSE's favour [E] (NUMBERS, CALL Aug 2026).
**The model treats working capital as neutral,** which is more favourable than the observed reality of a draining customer float and -Rs 290 cr of FY26 operating cash flow [F] (NUMBERS).

**Cash is not netted from enterprise value.** EV is market capitalisation plus borrowings, with no deduction for the Rs 3,511 cr cash balance, which is 13.1% of market capitalisation [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING), [E]. This is the single most important pro-company adjustment an investor could argue for, and we treat it as a genuine counter-argument rather than dismissing it - see the next section.

**Three-quarters of the value is terminal.** Rs 5,012.9 cr of the Rs 6,771.3 cr base-case enterprise value is the present value of the terminal value [F] (NUMBERS), [E]. For a business whose revenue comes from discrete eight-year programmes awarded by competitive tender, a Gordon perpetuity at 5.5% is a heroic construct in either direction - it could as easily overstate as understate [AI].

**Translate 65.2% for five years into rupees and the arithmetic becomes concrete [E].** Compounding Rs 7,507 cr of trailing revenue at 65.2% for five years gives year-five sales of approximately **Rs 92,400 cr** [E] (NUMBERS). For scale: that is roughly **6.8 times the entire current order book, every year**; it is about **60% of the entire Rs 1,50,000 cr AoN-accorded defence pipeline, every year**; and it is more than six times the Rs 15,000 cr a year that the company's own management discussion puts on the whole Indian defence shipbuilding market [F] (AR2025 p.80), [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [E]. It is not a demanding assumption. It is an arithmetically unavailable one on the disclosed size of the market.

The comparison that matters most is against the bull case. The bull scenario already assumes 43.5% starting growth fading to 13%, a 10% EBITDA margin - close to the best GRSE has ever achieved - and it still produces Rs 1,032.0 per share, 55.9% below the current price [F] (NUMBERS). **The price is not discounting the bull case. It is discounting something above the bull case, by a factor of 2.3x** [E] (NUMBERS).

**Set against the business as disclosed, the required growth runs in the opposite direction to the evidence [AI].** The price requires 65% annual sales growth for five years. The order book, which is the only contractual source of that revenue, has fallen 40% in fifteen months, from Rs 22,681 cr to Rs 13,596 cr, with approximately nil net new intake over the period [E] (NUMBERS, AR2025 p.44, CALL Aug 2026). Coverage has compressed from about 4.5 years of revenue to about 1.8 years [E]. The two projects generating 47% of the remaining backlog both complete in FY27, and the replacement contract - which would be the largest single order in GRSE's history - remains unsigned after more than twenty months at L1 and would contribute nothing before FY28 [MC] (CALL Aug 2026, CALL May 2026). Management itself has described FY27 as 'the peak year' and has declined to promise that FY28 will not decline [MC] (CALL Feb 2026, CALL May 2026).

Layer on the cash evidence: over three years GRSE reported Rs 1,632 cr of profit and generated -Rs 981 cr of operating cash, a conversion of -0.60x, with free cash flow negative in four of five years [F] (NUMBERS). A quarter to two-fifths of pre-tax profit is interest earned on a customer float that is draining by construction as the order book converts to revenue [E] (NUMBERS, AR2025 p.177). And a disclosed Rs 100 cr of FY25 profit, flagged by the auditor in an Emphasis of Matter, came from a revision to management's estimate of cost to complete, with a further unquantified provision reversal benefiting FY26 per the rating agency [F] (AR2025 p.141, p.199), [F] (RATING).

**The forensic conclusion is therefore narrow and specific: the valuation is not supported by anything in the disclosed evidence base.** Every scenario in the model - including a bull case assuming margins at record levels and growth above the recent run rate - sits between 56% and 94% below the current price, and the sensitivity grid cannot close the gap at any plausible discount rate [F] (NUMBERS), [E]. This is a statement about the relationship between price and disclosed fundamentals; it is not a rating and not a price target.

items: **1. The enterprise value is overstated because cash is not netted off.** EV is defined as market capitalisation plus borrowings; our statements data explicitly notes that the public source does not split cash out of other assets, so the Rs 3,511 cr cash balance is not deducted [F] (NUMBERS), [F] (RATING). That is 13.1% of market capitalisation [E]. A cash-adjusted EV would lower the implied growth requirement. It would not lower it anywhere near 20%, but the direction of the error is genuinely against the company [AI].

**2. The base-case margin is demonstrably too low.** An 8.0% base EBITDA margin against 11.4% achieved is a material understatement, and the model's own bull case at 10.0% is still below the FY26 outcome [F] (NUMBERS). A model run at the achieved margin would produce a higher base value. Again, the bull case tells you the size of that effect - and it is not enough [AI].

**3. A 15% WACC is high for a AAA-rated, 74.5% government-owned, net-cash company.** The sensitivity grid at 13.5% raises the base value to Rs 654.6-784.5 [F] (NUMBERS). Still 66-72% below the price [E].

**4. The order book genuinely understates contracted opportunity.** GRSE is L1 on a Rs 33,000 cr project with price negotiations complete and, per the rating agency, formal signature awaited [F] (RATING). Adding it would take the book to Rs 46,596 cr and coverage to about 6.2 years of trailing revenue [E]. That is a real, evidenced, near-certain addition that no order book snapshot captures - and it is the strongest single argument the bulls have [AI].

**5. A five-year DCF is a poor instrument for a business with eight-to-fifteen-year programme cycles.** The NGC completes in 2034-35; the P-17 Bravo, if won, would run a decade; the Navy's stated programme is 150-plus warships over 15 years [MC] (CALL Aug 2026), [F] (AR2025 p.80). A model that fades growth to 10% by year five and then applies a 5.5% perpetuity may systematically mis-time a lumpy, long-cycle revenue stream in both directions [AI].

**6. The government-ownership floor.** The rating agency's negative triggers include a substantial decline in GoI stake and a policy change increasing competition - i.e. the state's strategic commitment is an explicit rating support [F] (RATING). A business that cannot easily be disintermediated by the state may deserve a lower cost of capital and a higher terminal multiple than a generic contractor [AI].

blocks.text: **Our assessment of the counter-arguments [AI].** Points 1 to 3 are individually correct and collectively insufficient - the model's own bull case and its most generous sensitivity corner both remain more than half below the price. Point 4 is the genuinely strong one, and it is why we treat the NGC signature as the single most important near-term monitorable in this report. Point 5 is fair and cuts both ways: a long-cycle business can be undervalued by a five-year fade, and can equally be overvalued by a perpetuity that assumes the state keeps ordering at a constant real rate forever. Point 6 is real but is an argument about survival, not about growth, and the reverse DCF is a growth question.

subsections.title: Theme 1 - Order intake and the backlog

items: 1. The order book fell from Rs 22,681 cr at 31 Mar 2025 to Rs 13,596 cr at 30 Jun 2026 while about Rs 8,817 cr of revenue was recognised, implying net new order inflow of approximately nil over fifteen months. Can you confirm the gross order intake figure for FY26 and Q1 FY27, and commit to disclosing order intake alongside order book each quarter?

2. In November 2025 and again in February 2026 you guided to a year-end FY26 order book 'plus Rs 50,000 crores' and described it as 'assured'. The actual was Rs 15,324 cr. What changed, and what has changed in your internal forecasting process as a result?

3. On the Q1 FY27 call the shipbuilding order book was given as Rs 13,296 cr in the opening remarks and Rs 12,980 cr in the Q&A, while the itemised project list sums to Rs 12,640 cr. Which is correct, and what accounts for the Rs 340 cr difference between the itemised list and the stated total?

4. Are the four ONGC Platform Support Vessels and the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port green tug included in the Rs 13,596 cr order book at 30 Jun 2026, given that both were described as letters of intent rather than signed contracts?
5. The Mine Countermeasure Vessel AoN value was stated as Rs 32,000 cr on three consecutive calls and Rs 36,000 cr on the Q1 FY27 call. What drove the Rs 4,000 cr revision?

subsections.title: Theme 2 - The Next Generation Corvette and the FY28 bridge

items: 6. The NGC contract date has now been guided four times - within 3-4 months (Nov 2025), next month (Feb 2026), the June quarter (May 2026) and the current quarter (Aug 2026). What specific approval remains outstanding, with which authority, and what is the escalation path?

7. P-17A and ASW-SWC together are 47% of the order book and both complete in FY27. NGC revenue begins in FY28 and is material only from FY29. Quantify the FY28 revenue bridge: how much comes from base-and-depot spares, how much from NGOPV, how much from research vessels, how much from commercial vessels, and how much from orders not yet won?

8. You have said base-and-depot spares are 10-15% of project cost and are delivered after ship handover. What is the total contracted value of base-and-depot spares outstanding across all projects at 30 Jun 2026, and what margin do they carry relative to construction?
9. If the NGC contract is not signed by 31 March 2027, what happens to FY28 and FY29 revenue, and would you then revisit the commercial and export order intake you have consciously paused?
10. In the P-17 Bravo, if GRSE is L2 rather than L1, it receives three ships rather than four. What is the value difference, and at what point does an L2 outcome cease to bridge the gap?

11. Note 48 of the FY25 accounts and the auditor's Emphasis of Matter disclose that a revision of cost to completion on P-17A and NGOPV reduced cost to complete by Rs 433.03 cr and increased FY25 profit by Rs 100 cr. Was there an equivalent revision in FY26, and if so, what was its P&L effect?
12. Your rating agency states that the FY26 PBILDT margin 'benefited from reversal of excess cost provisions created in earlier years for ongoing projects'. Please quantify that benefit for FY26.

13. Adjusting for both the cost-to-complete revision and the provision reversals, what was the underlying EBITDA margin in FY25 and FY26? An analyst has now put this question to you twice and received the answer 'similar margins'.
14. Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin was 8.2% against 11.4% for FY26 and 16.8% for Q4 FY26. What margin do you expect for FY27 as a whole, and what would have to happen in Q2-Q4 to deliver it?
15. What is the contracted margin on the Next Generation Corvette relative to P-17A, given that P-17A was a nominated award and NGC was won in competition?

subsections.title: Theme 4 - Cash, working capital and the balance sheet

items: 16. Over FY24-FY26 GRSE reported Rs 1,632 cr of profit and generated -Rs 981 cr of operating cash flow. How much of that gap is the unwinding of customer stage payments, and what operating cash flow do you expect in FY27?
17. The GST receivable rose from Rs 926.42 cr to Rs 1,191.00 cr during FY25. What is the ageing of that balance, when do you expect it to be recovered, and what is it as at 31 Mar 2026?
18. Advances to suppliers rose from Rs 338.64 cr to Rs 539.55 cr during FY25. What projects do these relate to, and what is the ageing?
19. Debtor days rose from 19 in FY25 to 64 in FY26 against a prior three-year average of about 15. Which customers, and is any balance overdue by more than a year?

20. Contract liabilities fell from Rs 7,327 cr to Rs 6,900 cr in FY25 and cash fell from Rs 3,732 cr to Rs 3,511 cr in FY26. Your rating agency's negative trigger is liquid funds below Rs 3,000 cr on a continued basis. What is the floor you are managing to, and what happens to the Rs 246 cr of annual interest income as the float unwinds?

subsections.title: Theme 5 - Capital allocation, capacity and disclosure

items: 21. You have described about Rs 4,400 cr of expansion capex across four facilities. Your rating agency, writing six weeks earlier, recorded 'planned Rs 500-600 crore capex in the next two years'. Please reconcile the two figures and give a year-by-year cash capex profile for FY27 to FY31.

GRSE was carrying 40-44 platforms under construction against a stated 28-platform capacity. What proportion of platform-years is outsourced to partner yards, and will you publish a utilisation measure?

23. GRSE is exempt from segment reporting under Ind AS 108 and from detailed related-party disclosure under Ind AS 24. Nothing prevents voluntary disclosure. Will you publish divisional revenue and margin, and top-five customer concentration, even in an aggregated form that preserves security?

24. Ship repair revenue rose from Rs 19 cr to Rs 113.82 cr in three years and you have said its margins are high and that you 'have not gone all out'. What is the ship repair EBITDA margin, what capacity do the leased dry docks represent, and what revenue could the vertical reach by FY29?

You attribute this to the Presidential-Order appointment process. What specific representations has the board made to the Ministry of Defence, when, and what timeline have you been given?

items: **The strong outcome.** The NGC signs in FY27; the P-17 Bravo RFP lands and GRSE takes four or three ships; the MCMV and LPD follow; the Gujarat and Raichak yards open around FY30-31 and open the large-commercial segment; ship repair and the naval gun scale into genuine second and third verticals; margin holds above 10% through an equipment-heavy NGC cycle. This is broadly the model's bull case - 43.5% starting growth fading to 13%, a 10% margin - which the model values at Rs 1,032.0 per share [F] (NUMBERS).

**The central outcome.** FY27 is the peak year management has described. FY28 plateaus or dips on base-and-depot spares, the NGOPV and research vessels. The NGC signs late and ramps from FY29. GRSE wins some but not all of the pipeline, at competitive-tender margins. Capacity expansion proceeds slowly and absorbs cash. Revenue compounds in the high teens to low twenties from a FY27 peak. This is broadly the model's base case at Rs 587.9 [F] (NUMBERS).

**The weak outcome.** Programme approvals continue to slip as they have for twenty months; the NGC signs but with the ramp pushed into FY30; P-17 Bravo goes elsewhere or is split unfavourably; the margin reverts toward the FY22-24 range as estimate revisions stop; the customer float unwinds fully, taking both cash flow and interest income with it; the greenfield programme absorbs Rs 4,400 cr against a shrinking revenue base. This is broadly the model's bear case at Rs 148.8 [F] (NUMBERS).

**What would surprise us in either direction [AI].** On the upside: a genuine commercial shipbuilding breakthrough with disclosed margins, or a government decision to return to nomination-based awards for strategic programmes. On the downside: an unfavourable cost-to-complete revision, which would reverse the mechanism that lifted FY25 profit, or a disinvestment announcement that changed the ownership premise on which the rating and the strategic position rest.

subsections.title: Where the price sits and what drives the gap

blocks.text: The share price of Rs 2,340 sits above every fair value our DCF model produces. It is 4.0x the base case of Rs 587.9, 2.3x the bull case of Rs 1,032.0 and 15.7x the bear case of Rs 148.8 [F] (NUMBERS), [E]. The sensitivity grid, which spans Rs 472.0 to Rs 784.5 across a 300 basis point range of WACC and a 200 basis point range of terminal growth, does not contain a value within 66% of the price [F] (NUMBERS), [E]. The reverse DCF isolates the reason: today's enterprise value requires about 65.2% annual sales growth for five years, against 19.8% in the base case and 43.5% starting growth (fading to 13%) in the bull case [F] (NUMBERS).

**What drives the gap [AI].** Three things, in order of size. First, growth: the model fades growth from 30%, the market appears to be extrapolating the 38-44% of the last three years indefinitely, and the order book says neither is currently funded by contracts. Second, margin: the model's base uses 8% against 11.4% achieved, which understates value - but correcting it only takes you to the bull case, still 56% below. Third, the model's construction: enterprise value does not net Rs 3,511 cr of cash, a 15% WACC is high for a AAA-rated, state-owned, net-cash company, and a five-year fade with a 5.5% perpetuity is a crude instrument for eight-to-fifteen-year programme cycles. Those three construction points are real and legitimate, and together they narrow the gap without closing it. **The residual - the part that no adjustment to the model explains - is a market view that the Rs 1,50,000 cr pipeline converts into GRSE revenue at a rate and on a timetable that nothing in the disclosed evidence supports.**

This is a research view, not a recommendation. **No buy, sell, hold, overweight or underweight rating is offered, and no price target is set.** What we have done is establish where the price sits relative to a disclosed set of scenario values, and identified the specific, measurable evidence that would move the assessment in either direction.

subsections.title: Investment horizon and when to re-review

items: **Horizon.** This is a business whose outcome is decided on multi-year procurement cycles, not quarters. The decisive events - NGC signature and ramp, the P-17 Bravo award, the FY28 bridge, and the greenfield yards - resolve over three to five years. An investor evaluating GRSE on anything shorter than three years is effectively trading the DAC calendar [AI].

**Re-review trigger 1 - the NGC contract.** Re-review immediately on signature or on a fifth missed date by 31 Dec 2026. Signature would change the order book from Rs 13,596 cr to about Rs 46,600 cr and materially change the revenue-visibility assessment [E] (CALL Aug 2026, RATING).

**Re-review trigger 2 - Q2 FY27 results, expected in the second week of November 2026** [F] (AR2025 p.102). Two data points matter: the EBITDA margin, which must average about 12.5% across Q2-Q4 to deliver the guided 'similar' full-year figure against the 8.2% Q1 print [E] (NUMBERS); and the order book, which will show whether Q1's approximately Rs 87 cr of net intake was an aberration.

**Re-review trigger 3 - the FY26 annual report, circulated from 3 Sep 2026** [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS). This is the first sight of FY26 audited notes. Specifically: whether an Emphasis of Matter recurs; the size of any FY26 cost-to-complete revision; the movement in guarantee-repair, onerous-contract and other provisions; contract liabilities; the receivable ageing behind 64 debtor days; the GST receivable and supplier-advance balances; and the FY26 cash flow statement.

**Re-review trigger 4 - the P-17 Bravo RFP.** Its issue, and GRSE's L-position on award, is the single largest determinant of the FY29-FY34 revenue base on management's own framing: 'that is what will keep the company moving for another 10 years, 8 years' [MC] (CALL Feb 2026).

**Re-review trigger 5 - the next CARE rating action.** The agency's negative triggers are a continuous decline in order book and margin, and liquid funds below Rs 3,000 cr on a continued basis. Two of these are live. A rating outlook change would be a third-party confirmation of the order-book concern [F] (RATING).

**Re-review trigger 6 - board composition.** Appointment of the requisite Independent Directors including a Woman Independent Director would cure five years of non-compliance, unlock the Rs 2.30 cr fine waiver, and restore a properly constituted Audit Committee [F] (AR2025 p.100-101).
